_comment: How each place of the catalogue's words-06.jsonl was settled before it went in config/figures-seen/: two readers read every place against its BSB verse, one asking whether the figure is plainly there and one whether the marked words, form and tags are right; a place both passed is kept as handed over, and any place either questioned was read a third time and kept, changed or dropped. A new form stands only where a reader proposed it. Places not read are held, not listed.

Last, a sample of 25 kept places was read by two more readers, a third settling any split; the file goes in only when 24 or more pass, and any place that fails is dropped. "samples" lists each sample and its result.

Strong's tags are also taken off any kept place whose tags light the article (G3588) or the object marker (H0853), or number eight, the search's limit, or whose roots light more words of the verse than there are tags, or, on a question or parallel lines, that were chosen for marked words since changed: such tags are a stretch of words, or name words no longer marked.

Then, after a review of the build checks, every kept place was checked again as the build now checks it: overlapping entries were joined, so the place marks the same words ("overlapping entries joined"), and any place the build would refuse was dropped ("refused on the later checks").
A place whose verse already has the same form from an earlier file is left out here, since the earlier file's place stands ("same form already on this verse").

places.why: The serpent's "Did God really say...?" is answered as a real question by the woman in 3:2. That it hints rather than asks is a reading the verse does not plainly show.
Adam answers both questions in 3:12. Saying God asks only to draw a confession is commentary, not what the words plainly show.

"What is this you have done?" could be read as a rebuke, but the verse treats it as a real question in God's questioning of the pair: the woman answers it with her account, "The serpent deceived me," she replied, "and I ate." Taking it as a question that does not ask relies on what God already knows, which is inference rather than something the words plainly show, so it is in doubt and fails.

4:5 has already given the cause, and God's speech runs straight on into 4:7 without waiting for an answer, so the questions reprove rather than ask. The words are trimmed to the two questions, leaving out the speech tag "said the LORD to Cain".

"If you do what is right, will you not be accepted?" plainly means "you will be". The words are fixed to drop the stray leading comma. The tag H3808 also catches the lo' at word 5 ("if you refuse"), which is not part of the question.
Cain's "Am I my brother's keeper?" is a defiant denial that expects no. The words are trimmed to remove the stray ". “" at the start.
Coming after "Far be it from You!", the question plainly asserts that He will do right. The words are trimmed to remove the leading "!".

Lot has just said "it is a small place", so "is it not a small place?" argues rather than asks. The extra spans are not the question. Every tag sits on those other words, and the ha-lo' (H3808) that carries the question is untagged.
Between "Come" and "I have prepared the house", the question urges the man to come in and asks for no reason; he simply comes in (24:32). The words are trimmed to the question alone.

"Is he not rightly named Jacob?" plainly asserts that the name fits. The spans "So Esau declared" and "For he has cheated me twice" are not the question. The tags include both "and he said" (H0559) and H6117, H2088 and H6471, none of which carry the question.
Followed by "Tell me what your wages should be", the question plainly means "you should not". The words now take in the whole question and drop the stray leading comma.

Jacob can see what was done ("there was Leah!"), and he knows he served for Rachel (29:18), so these two questions plainly reproach rather than ask. "Why have you deceived me?" is left out because Laban answers it in 29:26. The narrative spans are removed. All the tags sit on the narrative, and mah and ha-lo' are untagged.
Laban's "Why did you run away secretly...?" is an accusation, but Jacob answers it with his reason in 31:31 ("I was afraid..."). It may be a real demand for an answer, so it is not plain.
"But why have you stolen my gods?" is a real charge that wants an answer: Jacob answers it and Laban searches the tents. The span also takes in the preceding statement.

"Will not their livestock, their possessions, and all their animals become ours?" is plainly a persuading question that expects yes. The extra spans and every tag, including the interrogative ha-lo' (H3808), lie inside the question clause.

The verse itself says "his father rebuked him", and his questions plainly mean no; he has just heard the dream and explains it himself. The words are trimmed to the two questions, leaving out the narration.

"Don't interpretations belong to God?" plainly asserts that they do. The extra spans are the officials' words. Every tag sits on those words and on "and he said to them", while the ha-lo' (H3808, word 10) is untagged.
The question rebukes the sons for doing nothing and asks for no reason, and 42:2 follows with "Go down there and buy some". The words are trimmed to remove the narration before it.

Reuben's "Didn't I tell you...?" plainly reminds them that he did. The spans "And Reuben responded" and "But you would not" are not the question. The tags take in the speech tag (H6030B, H7205, H0853), both le'mor, and the second lo' in "you would not listen".

Joseph's two questions are plainly a rebuke and a claim, not requests for facts. The marks are cut down to the two questions (no "Joseph declared", no fragment). The tags fall on "said", "Joseph" and a second "who" outside the figure, so they are stripped.
"who dares to rouse him?" plainly means no one dares. The stray leading comma is trimmed.
"Am I in the place of God?" right after "Do not be afraid" plainly means "I am not". The stray ". " at the start is trimmed.

The LORD's questions answer themselves ("Is it not I, the LORD?"), so they are plainly not asking. The marks drop the speech frame "And the LORD said to him" and cover the three questions. The tags fall on "said", "Yahweh" and "to him" in the frame and leave out the "is it not", so they are stripped.
Pharaoh's question is plainly a rebuke, as "Get back to your labor!" shows. The mark is cut to the question alone and leaves out the frame and "Moses and Aaron,".
The verse calls this an appeal, and Pharaoh answers it in 5:17 ("You are slackers!"). It may be a protest, but it is not plainly a question that is not asking, so in doubt it does not go live.
"will they not stone us?" plainly means "they will stone us". The stray leading comma is trimmed.
"Why are you crying out to Me?" followed at once by "Tell the Israelites to go forward" is plainly a reproof, not a request for a reason. The frame "Then the LORD said to Moses," is taken out.
Moses' two questions are plainly a reproach. The mark leaves out the narration and the people's demand and covers only his two questions.
The verse calls it grumbling, and "to make us ... die of thirst" makes it plainly an accusation, not a request for a reason. The narration before it is taken out.
"Is the LORD among us or not?" voices real doubt and demands proof, and the verse calls it testing. It does not plainly make a point the speakers hold, so in doubt it does not go live.
Moses answers Jethro's question as a real one in 18:15 ("Because the people come to me to inquire of God"). The verse does not plainly show a question that is not asking.

Moses' "how then can it be known ... unless You go with us?" plainly means it cannot be known any other way, and the second question repeats the point. The marks are set to the two whole questions in place of the fragments "unless" and "How else will we". The tags all fall inside the questions' words, so they stay, though the questioning "not" is untagged.
The men are asking for a ruling, and Moses treats it that way ("Wait here until I find out what the LORD commands"). It is not plainly rhetorical.
The quoted cry "Who will feed us meat? For we were better off in Egypt!" is plainly a complaint, not a real question. The stray ": ‘" at the start is trimmed.
"Why did we ever leave Egypt?" comes after "you have rejected the LORD" and is plainly a complaint of regret. The mark is cut from the whole verse down to the question.

The two questions plainly claim that the LORD speaks through Miriam and Aaron too. The marks drop "they said" and the fragment "Does He not" and cover the two whole questions. The tags fall on "said" and on the "Yahweh" of "the LORD heard", outside the questions, so they are stripped.
"Why then were you unafraid to speak against My servant Moses?" is plainly a rebuke. The mark is cut to line 4 alone, since lines 1 to 3 are statements.

"would she not have been in disgrace for seven days?" plainly expects yes. The mark is now that one sentence, without the speech frame, the stray comma or the duplicate fragment. The tags fall on said/LORD/to/Moses/father/spit/face and leave the question word ha-lo untagged, so they are stripped.

Both questions are grumbling (14:2), not real requests to learn something. The statement "Our wives and children will become plunder" and the stray period are removed from the mark. The tags include the object marker and miss the second question's ha-lo, so they are stripped.
Followed at once by "This will not succeed!", the question is plainly a rebuke. The mark now starts at "Why" and drops the speech frame "But Moses said".
Coming after "You have taken too much upon yourselves!", the question is plainly an accusation. Only the question is marked now, not the whole verse with its narrative and statements.

"As for Aaron, who is he that you should grumble against him?" plainly means Aaron is not the one they oppose. The verse says they have "conspired against the LORD". The stray leading comma is trimmed.
The verse itself frames this as speaking "against God and against Moses", so the question is plainly a complaint. The mark now starts at "Why" and leaves out the narrative frame.

"Am I not the donkey you have ridden all your life until today?" plainly expects yes and tells Balaam what he already knows. The speech frame, the fragment "not the donkey" and Balaam's answer "No" are removed. The tags fall on said/donkey/to/Balaam and on Balaam's final "no", so they are stripped.

"Did I not send you an urgent summons?" plainly expects yes, and "Am I really not able to richly reward you?" plainly means he is able. "Why did you not come to me?" is left out because Balaam answers it in 22:38. The overlapping spans and the speech frame are removed, and the tags on said/Balak/to/Balaam are stripped.

"Should I not speak exactly what the LORD puts in my mouth?" plainly expects yes. The speech frame "But Balaam replied" and the redundant "Should I not" are removed. The tags on answered and said are stripped.
BSB lines 3 and 4 come right after "God is not a man, that He should lie" and plainly mean that He always acts and always fulfills. Each is one whole BSB line, and the stray ". " is trimmed.

"Did I not tell you that whatever the LORD says, I must do?" plainly expects yes. The speech frame and the overlapping fragment are removed. The tags on answered/Balaam/said/to/Balak/saying are stripped.
"like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?" plainly means no one dares. The stray leading comma is trimmed.

"Did I not already tell the messengers you sent me" opens a question that ends with "?" in 24:13. It plainly expects yes, since he did tell them in 22:18. The figure shows in the BSB too, so the "only in the original" note is wrong. "Balaam answered Balak" and "you sent me" are removed as separate marks. The tags on said/Balaam/to/Balak/to me/saying are stripped.

The only question is the Hebrew ha-loh hi ("is it not"), which the BSB gives as the plain statement "is still in Rabbah". That word is untagged. The tags and marks fall on the narrative "For only Og king of Bashan... Rephaim" and on "His bed of iron", which carry no question. Without its tags the place would label a BSB statement as a question, so it cannot go live.
After "ask now from one end of the heavens to the other", the question plainly expects no. The stray leading ": " is trimmed.

"Who will ascend into heaven to get it for us...?" is quoted as the question people would really need to ask if the command were far off, and the verse says they need not ask it. Inside the quote it is a real request for someone to go, so the verse does not plainly show a question that is not asking.

As in 30:12, "Who will cross the sea to get it for us...?" is the question people "should need to ask" if the word were far off. It is a real request, not plainly a question that tells, so it does not go live without a writer naming it.

The people's "Have not these disasters come upon us...?" states their own conclusion, so it plainly is not asking. The other spans ("On that day My anger will burn" and the rest) are statements. The tags sit on that first clause and miss the question word ha.Lo' (word 18).

Joshua's "why did You ever bring this people across the Jordan...?" is a lament, and "If only we had been content to stay" follows it. The span should start at "why" and leave out the address and speech tag.
"Stand up! Why have you fallen on your face?" is a rebuke, and God gives the reason Himself in 7:11. Only the question carries the figure, not "But the LORD said to Joshua" or "Stand up!".
"Why did you deceive us...?" demands an account, and the Gibeonites give their reason in 9:24. So it is not plain that the question asks nothing. The span also takes in the narrative.

"Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?" (poetry line 5) plainly affirms that it is written. The sun and moon spans are not the question. The tags sit on that clause, and ha.lo' (word 8) is untagged.
"Why have you given us only one portion...?" is a complaint seeking redress, and Joshua answers it in 17:15. It is not plain that it asks nothing, and the span takes in the speech tag.

"Was not Achan son of Zerah unfaithful...?" plainly states what everyone knew. "Yet it was not" belongs to the BSB's exclamation, not the question. H3808 also marks the later lo' (word 16), which the BSB renders as that exclamation, so the tag is dropped as doubtful.
The BSB has no question ("Surely the LORD... is commanding you"). The question is only in the Hebrew ha.Lo' (word 9), which is untagged. The marked words and the tags point at narrative and names.
"Has not the LORD gone before you?" plainly affirms that He has. The other spans are speech tag and command, not the question. The tags sit on those words and miss ha.Lo' (word 14).
"Dan, why did you linger by the ships?" (poetry line 2) is a reproach in the song, like 5:16. Line 1, "Gilead remained beyond the Jordan.", is a statement and should not be marked.

The fathers' words "Has not the LORD brought us up out of Egypt?" plainly affirm what He did. "Please", "my Lord" and "Gideon replied" are not the figure. The tags sit on those words, and ha.Lo' (word 20) is untagged.
"Am I not sending you?" plainly assures Gideon of his commission. The speech tag and the command are not the question. The tags sit on them and miss ha.Lo' (word 12).
Ephraim's "Why have you done this to us?" is an angry demand for an account, which Gideon answers in 8:2. It is not plain that it asks nothing, and the span takes in the speech tag.

Both of Gideon's questions plainly flatter Ephraim, and 8:3 repeats the first. "But Gideon answered them" is not the figure, and the first span opened with a stray "?". The tags include "said" and "to them".
"Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him?" is plain contempt, not an inquiry. "Then Gaal son of Ebed said" is not the figure. The tags sit on said, Gaal, son and Ebed.
"Where is your gloating now?" is a plain taunt. "Zebul replied" and "You said" are not the figure. The tags include said, to him, Zebul and asher.

The BSB words "The LORD replied, When the Egyptians" show no question, because the BSB puts it in 10:12 ("did I not save you"), which place 149 already marks. Most tags sit on said, Yahweh, people and Israel.

"Did you not hate me and expel me from my father's house?" plainly asserts a known wrong. The second question is answered by the elders in 11:8, so it is left out. The speech tag is not the figure, and only H3808 among the tags belongs.
"What do you have against me...?" is a diplomatic demand for a reason, and the king answers it with his claim in 11:13. It is not plain that it asks nothing.
"Why did you not take them back during that time?" argues that three hundred years of silence settle the claim, so it plainly is not asking. The statement before it is not the question.

Ephraim's "Why have you crossed over...without calling us?" is an accusation that Jephthah answers with his reasons in 12:2-3. It is not plain that it asks nothing, and the span takes in the narrative.
"Why then have you come today to fight against me?" closes Jephthah's case and means they have no cause. The statement before it is not the question and should not be marked.

"Did you invite us here to rob us?" is an accusation that comes with a threat, so it is plainly not asking, and it shows in the BSB. The other three spans are the narrative or the command, and the tags sit on those words instead of the question.

"Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she?" persuades, and "Please take her instead" follows. The span is trimmed of the stray ". ", the other spans are dropped, and the tags (said, father, hated, gave) miss the question.

"Do you not realize that the Philistines rule over us?" is a reproach: Samson knows it already. The narrative spans are dropped, and the tags fall on "went down", "three thousand", "Judah" and "rock" instead of the question.

The weeping people cry "Why... has this happened in Israel?" to the LORD. It reads as a lament, but it can also be a real plea to God for an answer, and the span takes in the narrative "they cried out". There is doubt, so it does not go live.

The BSB has no question here ("Indeed, I have ordered the young men"). The Hebrew halo before "have I commanded" is often just "surely", so a question figure is not plain even in the original, and most of the spans and tags are on unrelated words.

"Now is not Boaz... a relative of ours?" asserts what Naomi had already told Ruth (2:20), and the BSB shows the question, so the note that it shows only in the original is wrong. The span "Now is not" is widened to the whole question, and the tag on "now" does not carry it.

"Am I not better to you than ten sons?" plainly asserts and comforts. The span is trimmed of the stray "? ". "Hannah" and "her husband Elkanah asked" are dropped, and so are the less certain "why" questions. The tags fall on said, Elkanah, husband and Hannah.
"Did I not clearly reveal Myself to your father's house...?" asserts what the LORD did, and v28 goes on to state it. The span is trimmed of the leading ": '".
After "Woe to us!", "Who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods?" is a cry of despair meaning no one can. The span is trimmed of the stray "! ".

"Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs?" is a warning not to, and "did they not send the people on their way...?" recalls a history everyone knew. The overlapping fragments and the lone "When" are dropped. The tags sit on object markers, names and "when".

"And upon whom is all the desire of Israel, if not upon you...?" plainly asserts that it is on Saul, and the BSB shows it. The donkey spans are dropped, the question is given whole, and every tag sits on the donkey clause.

"Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe..., and is not my clan the least...?" is a humble assertion, not a request. "Saul replied" and the lone "not" are dropped, and the tags on answered, Saul and said are wrong.

"Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?" plainly declares the anointing that Samuel has just performed. The narrative spans are dropped, and all the tags (took, Samuel, flask, oil, poured, head, over) miss the question.
After "How much better it would have been", "Would not the slaughter of the Philistines have been much greater?" plainly asserts that it would have. The span is trimmed of the stray "! ".
"Why have You not answered Your servant this day?" is a real appeal to God for the cause, which Saul goes straight on to seek by Urim, Thummim and the lot. It is not plainly a question that tells.
"Must Jonathan die...? Never!" is a question the people answer themselves. The span was the whole verse and is narrowed to the question alone.

"Although you were once small in your own eyes, have you not become the head of the tribes of Israel?" plainly asserts it. The span now covers the whole question, without the stray comma, "And Samuel said" or the lone "not". The tags on said and Samuel are wrong.

"Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obedience to His voice?" is answered at once: "Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice". The span is trimmed of the colon and quote mark so that it is exactly the BSB's poetry lines 2 and 3.
"How can I go?" may be an objection, but the LORD answers it with a way to go ("Take a heifer with you"), so it can be read as a real question. It is not plain.

Goliath's "Why do you come out and array yourselves for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul?" is a taunt that seeks no answer. The narrative and the lone "Am" are dropped, and the tags fall on stood, called, battle lines, Israel and said.

Eliab's "Why have you come down here?" and "And with whom did you leave those few sheep...?" are rebukes, and he answers them himself ("you have come down to see the battle!"). The span was the whole verse and is narrowed to the two questions.

David's "What have I done now?" protests Eliab's charge and his "Was it not just a question?" means "it was only a word". Neither asks for information. The marks repeated the question and added "said David", and the tags fell on said and David as well.
Goliath's "Am I a dog ... that you come at me with sticks?" is a scornful question, plainly not asking. It is marked as two spans so the narrator's "he said to David" is left out.
After "Never!", "would I not tell you?" means "I would surely tell you". The span is trimmed of the stray ". “" left over from the sentence before.
Jonathan's "will I not send for you and tell you?" is a promise under oath, put as a question. The span now starts at "If he is favorable" and drops the stray comma.

"Do I not know ...?" is Saul saying he knows well, not asking. The narration ("Then Saul’s anger burned", "and he said"), the insult and the stray "!" are dropped. The tags covered those words and missed halo' yada'ti.

This is the sign agreed in 20:22. Jonathan knows where he shot the arrow, so "Isn’t the arrow beyond you?" tells and does not ask. The narration spans are dropped. The tags sat on that narration and missed halo'.

The servants use both questions to tell Achish who this man is. The narration "But the servants of Achish said to him", the bare "David" and the fragment "they not sing" are dropped. The tags also fell on said, servants, Achish, to him and le'mor.
"Why have you brought him to me?" is Achish's rebuke, plainly not asking. Only the question is marked now, without the narration or the statement "Look, you can see that the man is insane!".

The Ziphites are telling Saul where David is hiding, and 23:20 goes on with their offer to hand him over. The narration span and the repeated "Is not" are dropped. Most of the tags fell on the narration (went up, Ziphites, Saul, Gibeah, saying).
David's "Why do you listen ...?" is a plea for Saul to stop listening, not a request for a reason. The narration "and said to Saul," is dropped.
The run of questions, answered by "A dead dog? A flea?", plainly shows that Saul's pursuit is pointless. The old span began with a stray "?" and left out the questions around it.
The Ziphites are telling Saul where David is, and in 26:2 he goes to search there. The narration span and the repeated "Is not" are dropped. Most of the tags fell on the narration.

David shouts "Will you not answer me, Abner?" to get Abner to reply, and Abner does reply ("Who calls to the king?"). It really asks for an answer, so the figure is not plain. The spans and tags were also on the narration.

David's three questions taunt Abner for failing to guard the king, and 26:16 spells out the charge. "So David said to Abner" is dropped. The tags fell on said, David, to and Abner, and on 'el-, as well as on the question particles.

"Why have you set a trap to get me killed?" is the woman's accusation, and Saul answers it with an oath, not a reason. Only the question is marked now, without the narration or the statement before it.
"Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!" is an outcry of accusation, not a request for a reason. The narration before the question is dropped.

Saul answers "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" as a real question and gives his reason ("So I have called on you to tell me what to do"). The figure is not plain, and the span also took in the narration.
"Why do you consult me ... since the LORD has turned away from you?" means there is no use asking. It is marked as two spans so the narrator's "asked Samuel" is left out.

Achish's "Is this not David ...?" states who David is and vouches for him, as the rest of the verse shows. The commanders' words and the narration spans are dropped. The tags fell on those words and left halo' untagged.

The marked words were narration and commands with no question in them. The verse does plainly show the figure in the commanders' "What better way for him to regain the favor of his master than with the heads of our men?", meaning he would win Saul back with their heads. It is kept with that question as its words, and it shows in the BSB, not only in the Hebrew. The tags followed the wrong words.

"Is this not the David about whom they sing ...?" plainly asserts that this is the David of the song, and it shows in the BSB, not only in the Hebrew. A lone "not" did not show the question. The H3808 tag on halo' is right.
"Why were you not afraid ...?" is a condemnation: David has the man executed without waiting for an answer. The span now runs to the end of the question, which had been cut off at "the LORD".
"Where should I go?" is a real question David puts to the LORD, and the LORD answers it: "To Hebron." There is no figure.

Abner's three questions plainly urge Joab to stop the pursuit (2:27). The marked words had a stray ": “" and the narrative "Then Abner called out to Joab". The tags fall on called, Abner, to, Joab and said, and miss the halo' that carries the second question.
An indignant denial, answered by "All this time I have been loyal". Trimmed the stray ". “" in front of the question.

Joab's questions plainly rebuke the king and are not asking for facts. The span also took in the narrative "So Joab went to the king and said" and the statement "Look, Abner came to you.", so only the two questions are marked now.
The question states what everyone knows. "Then the king said to his servants" is narrative. Its tags (said, king, to, servants) do not carry the figure. Only halo' does.

The Hebrew halo' avaqqesh asks "shall I not require" to mean "I surely will", and the BSB keeps the question's shape. The if-clause and "How much more" are only the condition. The tags fall on that clause and on object markers, and miss halo' and "require".
David asks in fear. He is voicing dread, not asking how to do it, and 6:10 shows he would not move the ark. The narrative "That day David feared the LORD and asked" is no longer marked.

Both questions plainly accuse David rather than ask. The marks had the narrative "the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun their lord", "Just because David has sent", "comforters" and a stray "? ", and they missed the first question. Most tags fall on said, leaders, Ammon and Hanun, and halo' is untagged.

The BSB has no question here, only the answer "This is Bathsheba...". The Hebrew halo' may simply mean "surely" in a plain reply, so the figure is not plain. All the marked words and nearly all the tags are narrative.

David knows the answer and asks to press Uriah to go home. "And David was told" and "Uriah did not go home" are the report. Uriah answers "Why didn't you go home?" (11:11), so it is left unmarked. The tags fall on the report and the speech formula.

The king's foreseen questions are plainly rebukes. "if the king's anger flares", "he may ask" and a stray "? " are not the figure. The tags fall on it-will-be, if, rise, anger, king and say, and halo' is untagged.

The questions recall a story everyone knows (Abimelech and the millstone) to rebuke, and the marked span is the three questions. But the tags take in the object marker and the names Abimelech and Jerubbesheth, which do not carry the figure.
"Why should he go with you?" may be a real, reluctant or suspicious question, and Absalom answers by urging him (13:27). The verse does not plainly show that it is not asking.

"Have I not commanded you?" plainly asserts Absalom's authority to reassure his men. The other marked spans are orders, not the figure. The tags fall on commanded, Absalom, servants, saying, look, please, good and object markers, and halo' is untagged.
The question expects yes and accuses the king. Trimmed the stray leading comma.

"Is this the loyalty you show your friend?" is a plain taunt. The span also ran through "Absalom replied" into "Why did you not go with your friend?", which Hushai answers (16:18), so only the first question is marked.

The question plainly means "the son, of course". "Furthermore", the later "I served" and a stray ", " are not the figure. The tags include the H8145 on "Furthermore", and the serve tag also lands on the later "I served".
Joab's question is a rebuke, not a request for a reason. The span also took in the exclamation "You just saw him!" and the narrative "Joab exclaimed."
Joab's question argues Ahimaaz out of running. The span covered the whole verse, including the narrative and Ahimaaz's plea.
The question plainly reproaches the people and urges them to act. The statement "But Absalom ... has died in battle" was also marked and is no longer.
"Aren't you my flesh and blood?" plainly asserts kinship. "And say to Amasa" is narrative, and the "not" belongs to the oath. Their tags (Amasa, say, the oath's lo') are wrong.

David's three questions rebuke Abishai and assert that no one will die (19:23). "And David replied" and the address "Sons of Zeruiah" are not the figure. The tags fall on said, David, sons, Zeruiah, every ki and every "today", and the halo' is untagged.
The question means he has no right left. The span covered the whole verse, including the statement before it.
Barzillai's "Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks?" plainly means "I cannot", in a run of age questions. The span began with a stray "? " from the question before.
"Have we ever eaten at the king's expense...?" plainly means "we have not". The span began with the stray "? " from "Why does this anger you?".

"Why then do you despise us? Were we not the first...?" are complaints put as questions and expect no answer. The span took in the narration and the statement "We have ten shares in the king". Only the two questions are marked now.
"Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?" plainly means "it is", which is why he pours it out. The span began with the stray "! " from "to do this!".

The Rabshakeh's "is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed...?" is plainly an argument, not a request to learn something, and the BSB shows it. The marks missed this question and are replaced with it. The tags sit on "if", "say", "to", "Yahweh", "God" and "trust", and the note that the figure shows only in the original is wrong, so the tags are stripped.

The question plainly means the message is also for the men on the wall, and the BSB shows this. "But the Rabshakeh replied" is no longer marked, and the whole question is. The tags on "and he said" and the title Rabshakeh do not carry the figure, so they are stripped.
The question is a boast that no god has delivered his land. The stray ".’" from the sentence before is removed from the mark.
"Who created all these?" points to the Creator, and the next line answers it ("He leads forth the starry host"). The stray ": " is removed from the mark.

"Do you not know? Have you not heard?" are plainly reproving questions. "He will not grow tired" is a statement, so it is no longer marked. H3808 also tags the two plain negatives in "will not grow tired or weary", so the tags are stripped.

The verse asks and answers its own question to make the point. The overlapping marks are cleaned up into the two questions. The tags also take in the plain negatives of "They were unwilling" and "would not obey", so they are stripped.

"Do you not see it?" calls them to notice what God is plainly doing; it is not asking. The stray ". " and the statements "I am about to do something new" and "even now it is coming" are no longer marked. The tags fall mostly on those statements' words, so they are stripped.

The question the idolater cannot bring himself to ask plainly means "this is a lie". The statements "He feeds on ashes", "His deluded heart has led him astray" and "and he cannot deliver himself or say" are no longer marked. The tags sit on those words and on the object marker, so they are stripped.
Both questions plainly expect no: the made thing has no right to question its maker. The mark began with a stray ". " and left out the matching second question, so both are marked now.

God asks and answers his own questions ("Was it not I, the LORD?") to make the point. The stray ". " and the commands "Speak up and present your case", "yes" and "let them take counsel together" are no longer marked. The tags fall on those commands' words and miss the question word, so they are stripped.
"Will you not acknowledge them?" presses them to admit what they have heard; it is not asking. The stray ". " is removed from the mark.

Zion's words "in her heart" read as real, astonished wondering about where the children came from, and 49:22 answers them. It is not plain that she asks only to make a point, so when in doubt the place stays out.

Right after "The One who vindicates Me is near", the question "Who will dare to contend with Me?" plainly means no one will. The span is trimmed to drop the stray ". " left over from the sentence before.
After "Surely the Lord GOD helps Me", the question "Who is there to condemn Me?" plainly means no one. The span is trimmed to drop the stray ". " from the sentence before.

"Who among you fears the LORD ... ? ... Let him trust in the name of the LORD" works as "whoever among you", a call to the hearer. It does not make a point through an implied answer, so the figure is not plain.

"Was it not You who cut Rahab to pieces...?" plainly expects a yes. "Awake, awake, put on strength" is a call, not the question, so those spans are removed. The tags sit on awake, put on, strength, arm, LORD and days, and leave the question word ha-lo untagged, so they are stripped.

After 57:3 calls them "sons of a sorceress", "Whom are you mocking? At whom do you snarl...?" plainly accuses them and asks nothing. The doubled span and the lone "not" are replaced with the two questions. The tags run over exactly these two Hebrew questions (al-mi ... ta'arikhu), so they point at the figure.

"Whom have you dreaded and feared...?" is a reproach, and "Is it not because I have long been silent...?" expects a yes. Both plainly make a point. The pieces and the bare "Is it not" are replaced with the two whole questions. The tags include the object marker three times, plus the plain negatives of "not remember" and "not fear", so they are stripped.

"Isn't this the fast that I have chosen ...?" plainly expects a yes, answering the questions of 58:5. The BSB itself sets it as a question, so the note that it shows only in the original is wrong, and the span becomes the whole question. The one tag, on ha-lo, is right.

"Isn't it to share your bread with the hungry ...?" plainly expects a yes. "and not" is an ordinary negative inside the question, so it is removed. The H3808 tag also sits on that later lo ("not hide yourself"), which has nothing to do with the question, so the tags are stripped.

Whether "Who are these...?" is a question of wonder or a real question that 60:9 answers is open to doubt. The likeness is plain, though: they "fly like clouds, like doves to their shelters". So the place is kept as a simile on those words.

"Who is this coming from Edom...?" is a question within a dialogue, and the one asked answers it in the same verse: "It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save." It is a real question in the scene, not one that tells.
"They did not ask, 'Where is the LORD who brought us up...?'" reports a question the people failed to ask. In their mouths it would have been a real seeking of God, not a question that makes a point.
"The priests did not ask, 'Where is the LORD?'" reports a question never asked. Asking it would have been a real seeking after God, not a question that tells.

"can he ever return to her?" plainly expects a no, and "Would not such a land be completely defiled?" plainly expects a yes. The fragments and the bare "Would not such" are replaced with the two whole questions. The tags fall on le'mor "saying", the object marker and the if-clause, and leave the question words ha-yashuv and ha-lo untagged, so they are stripped.

"Have you seen what faithless Israel has done?" is a prose opener: God draws the prophet's attention and then tells him. That it is a figure making a point by an implied answer is not plain enough without a commentary, so when in doubt it does not go live.

"O LORD, do not Your eyes look for truth?" plainly expects a yes, set against people who refuse correction. The address "O LORD" and the plain negative "but they felt no" do not carry the question, so the span becomes the question alone. The tags sit on LORD, eyes and the later ve-lo as well as ha-lo, so they are stripped.

"To whom can I give this warning? Who will listen to me?" plainly means no one will, as the next line shows: "Look, their ears are closed". The mark began with a stray "? ", so it now holds both questions, copied whole.
"Ask for the ancient paths: 'Where is the good way?' Then walk in it" is a real question the people are told to ask so they can find the way. It is not asked to make a point.

"But am I the One they are provoking? ... Is it not themselves they spite, to their own shame?" plainly makes a point. It does not ask. The marks repeated the first question, added "declares the LORD" and cut the second question short, so they now hold the two whole questions. The tags fall on the object markers and on "declares the LORD" (H5002, H3068G), which are not the figure, so they are dropped.

"Do men fall and not get up again? Does one turn away and not return?" expect the obvious answer that they do, and 8:5 then applies it to the people. The mark began with a stray ": “", so it now holds the two whole poetry lines.

"No one repents of his wickedness, asking, 'What have I done?'" reports a question of repentance that nobody asks. The speaker is not using a question to make a point, so the figure is not plain here.

The exiles' cry "Is the LORD no longer in Zion?" could be read as real bewilderment, so it is not plain. But the LORD's reply plainly is a question that tells: "Why have they provoked Me to anger with their carved images, with their worthless foreign idols?" is an accusation, not a request to learn why. The mark (which also began with a stray ": “") now holds His question.

"What will you say when He sets over you close allies whom you yourself trained?" and "Will not pangs of anguish grip you, as they do a woman in labor?" plainly tell rather than ask. The marks began with a stray "? " and held the fragment "Will not", so they now hold the two whole questions. The tags fall only on the first question, including the object marker H0853, and miss the second, so they are dropped.

"Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain? Do the skies alone send showers? Is this not by You, O LORD our God?" plainly says that only the LORD gives rain. The marks repeated the first question and cut the third to "Is this not", so they now hold the three whole questions. The tags fall on the words of the first two questions, which is right.
"If they ask you, 'Where shall we go?'" is a real question, and the LORD then answers it ("Those destined for death, to death..."). It is not asked to make a point.
"can I not treat you as this potter treats his clay?" is answered at once by "so are you in My hand", so it plainly asserts His right. The mark began with a stray ", ".
"Who has ever heard things like these? Virgin Israel has done a most terrible thing" plainly means no one has. The mark began with a stray ": ".

"Does it make you a king to excel in cedar? Did not your father have food and drink?" are plainly questions of rebuke. The marks began with a stray "? " and held the fragments "Does it make you a king", "in cedar" and "Did not your father", so they now hold the two whole questions. The tags all fall within the two questions.

"Is this not what it means to know Me?" plainly expects yes. The marks began with a stray ". " and added the statement "He took up the cause of the poor and needy", "and so" and a bare "not", so they now hold the question alone. The tags fall mostly on that statement (H1777, H1779, H6041, H0034, H0227A, H2895), not on the question, so they are dropped.

"But which of them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear His word? Who has given heed to His word and obeyed it?" plainly means none of the false prophets has. The mark began with a stray "? " and left out the first, matching question, so it now holds both.

The elders argue from a case everyone knows: Hezekiah did not kill Micah (answer no), and he did fear the LORD (answer yes). Both questions are plainly not asking. One marked span opened with a stray "?" and another was a fragment, so the words are now the two whole questions. Most tags sit on Hezekiah, king, Judah and all, which do not carry the figure, so the tags are stripped.
"Can a male give birth?" plainly expects no and sets up the picture of men "like a woman in labor". The span opened with a stray ": ", so it is now BSB line 2 alone.

Zedekiah's "Why are you prophesying like this?" may be a real demand for a reason, and in the BSB 32:6 opens "Jeremiah replied", which reads as an answer. So the verse does not plainly show a question that is not asking. The span also took in the narration "For Zedekiah king of Judah had imprisoned him, saying". When in doubt, drop.

God's "Have you not noticed what these people are saying...?" draws Jeremiah's attention and asks nothing. The tag H3808 rightly sits on the question word ha.Lo'. The mark covered only "Have you not", so it now covers the whole question, which the BSB also shows.

"Will you not accept discipline and obey My words?" is a reproach, as 35:14's "you have not obeyed Me" shows. The three extra spans mark the messenger formula, and every tag sits on thus, says, Yahweh, hosts, God, Israel, go or say, while the question word ha.Lo' is untagged. So the words are now the question alone and the tags are stripped.

Jehoiakim said this as he burned the scroll, so the question is an indignant rejection, not a request for a reason. The span covered the whole verse, including "You are to proclaim concerning Jehoiakim...", so it is now the quoted question alone.

The BSB has no question here ("you will surely put me to death"), and the Hebrew ha.Lo' before hamet temiteni can be read as an emphatic "surely", so the figure is not plain even in the original. None of the marked words ("If I tell you", "Jeremiah replied", "even if I", "will not listen") carry it. The tags sit on said, Jeremiah, to, Zedekiah, if, tell, the plain lo' of "not listen" and "to me".

God's "Why are you doing such great harm to yourselves...?" is plainly a reproach and asks nothing, and 44:8 goes on in the same way. The span took in the messenger formula "So now, this is what the LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel, says:", so it now starts at "Why".

"did the LORD not remember and bring this to mind?" expects yes, and 44:22 goes on "So the LORD could no longer endure". The tag H3808 rightly sits on ha.Lo'. The span opened with a stray dash, and the separate "not" span repeated a word inside it, so the words are now the question alone.

Both questions plainly expect yes and set up the contrast in 49:10, "But I will strip Esau bare". The span opened with a stray comma and left out the condition, so the words are now BSB lines 1 and 2 and the matching pair, lines 3 and 4.

The passers-by's "Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty...?" is plainly a taunt, said while they clap, hiss and shake their heads. The span covered the whole verse, so it is now BSB lines 5 to 7.

The BSB gives "Is not the time near to build houses?" as a question, but the Hebrew has no question word (plain lo' beqarov), and the line can just as well read as a statement, "the time is not near to build houses". So the figure rests on a disputed rendering rather than the plain words. With no writer behind it, it should not go live.

God's "hasn't the rebellious house of Israel asked you...?" expects yes and makes a point for Ezekiel's answer in 12:10. It asks nothing. The span opened with a stray comma, and one span marked the address "Son of man". Two of the three tags sit on ben and adam, which do not carry the figure, so the words are now the question alone and the tags are stripped.

Right after 13:6 says "They see false visions", the question "Haven't you seen a false vision...?" plainly accuses and does not ask. The extra spans "Haven't you" and "have not" are dropped. "have not" belongs to the plain negative "I have not spoken". The H3808 tag also lands on that second lo' (token 11), so the tags are stripped.

The BSB turns the outer question into a statement ("you will not be asked, 'Where is the whitewash...?'"), so a BSB reader cannot plainly see what the taunt does. It is in doubt. The tags on behold, fallen and wall, and the spans "Surely when the wall has fallen" and "you will not", do not carry the question.
It comes after "sacrificed them as food to idols", and "Was your prostitution not enough?" plainly rebukes; it asks for nothing. The stray leading period is trimmed from the span.
"Have you not committed this lewdness...?" is an accusation in question form that expects yes, following "I will surely bring your deeds down upon your own head". The stray leading period is trimmed.

The speaker answers his own questions at once ("All its foliage will wither!"), so they plainly tell rather than ask. The speech formula span "So you are to tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says" is dropped, along with the stray "?". Its tags (say, thus, Lord, Yahweh) and the H3808 on "and not by a great arm" do not carry the figure, so the tags are stripped.

The next line answers the questions: "It will wither on the bed where it sprouted." They plainly tell. The span is set to the two questions, without the stray "?" or the separate "Even if it is transplanted". The tags on behold and planted (H2009, H8362) are not the question, so the tags are stripped.

The question is put to a "rebellious house" as a reproach, and the speaker goes straight on to explain the meaning himself, so he waits for no answer. The spans "Now say to this rebellious house" and "Tell them" are dropped, and so are their tags (say, please, house, rebellion, say), so the tags are stripped.
The three questions all expect no, and 17:16 answers them: "he will die in Babylon". The span now takes all three questions without the stray leading "?".

Both questions plainly state God's will, and 18:32 says it outright: "I take no pleasure in anyone's death". The formula "declares the Lord GOD" and its tags (H5002, H0136, H3069) are not part of the question, so the tags are stripped and the spans are set to the two questions.

The two questions turn the people's charge back on them and ask for no answer. The spans "Yet you say", "The way of the Lord is not just" (the people's own statement) and "Hear now" are not the question, and the question's first half was missing. The tags cover the whole verse, so they are stripped.

The questions plainly rebuke and turn the charge back. "Yet the house of Israel says" and "The way of the Lord is not just" are the people's statement, not the question, and a stray "?" opened the span. The tags cover nearly every word, so they are stripped.

Ezekiel reports this as a complaint ("Ah, Lord GOD"), and the people's "Is he not just telling parables?" plainly brushes the prophet aside; it is not a wish to learn. The spans "Then I said", "Ah" and "Lord GOD" and their tags (said, alas, Lord, Yahweh, they, saying) are the frame around it, so the tags are stripped.

"And what if even the scepter, which the sword despises, does not continue?" is an obscure line, and a reader cannot plainly see what point it makes. The span ", does not continue?" is only a fragment.
"Won't you tell us what these things you are doing mean to us?" is a real request for an explanation, and Ezekiel gives one in 24:20 ("So I answered them..."). There is no figure.

The BSB has a plain statement ("And you, son of man, know that on the day..."), so the figure would show only in the Hebrew ha.lo', which reads here as "surely". It is not plain. The spans "And you", "son of man" and "daughters as well" and the tags on you, son, humankind and sons carry no question.

"Will not the coastlands quake...?" plainly means they will, and 26:16 goes on to describe the princes "trembling every moment". The speech formula span "This is what the Lord GOD says to Tyre" and its tags (thus, says, Lord, Yahweh, Tyre) are not the question, so the tags are stripped and the stray ": " is trimmed.
Inside a lament, "Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea?" means no one was; it does not ask. The span is the BSB's lines 3 and 4, with the colon of line 2 trimmed.
"How can we live?" may be a cry of despair, but it can as well be a real question, and God answers it in 33:11 ("turn from their ways and live"). It is in doubt, so it stays out.

After the list of sins ("You eat meat with the blood in it... and shed blood"), "Should you then possess the land?" plainly means they should not, and it answers the boast of 33:24. The stray leading period is trimmed.
The repeated question follows "each of you has defiled his neighbor's wife" and plainly means they should not. The stray leading period is trimmed.

"Should not the shepherds feed their flock?" plainly rebukes the shepherds "who only feed themselves" and expects yes. The spans "Son of man", "prophesy against" and "of Israel" and their tags are the address, not the question, and the interrogative ha.Lo' (token 21) is untagged, so the tags are stripped and the stray "!" is trimmed.
"Son of man, can these bones come to life?" is a real, open question in the dialogue, and Ezekiel answers it ("O Lord GOD, only You know"). It does not make a point by an unspoken answer.
"Won't you explain to us what you mean by these?" is the people's real request for an explanation, and 37:19 gives it. There is no figure.

"will you not take notice of this?" plainly means Gog will, and 38:15 goes on: "And you will come from your place". The span now takes the whole question without the stray comma. The spans "Therefore prophesy", "son of man" and "and tell Gog that this is what the Lord GOD says", and all eight tags, are on the speech formula, while ha.Lo' (token 10) is untagged, so the tags are stripped.
"Son of man, do you see this?" draws the prophet's attention to the river. Whether it makes a point rather than simply asking is not plain, so it stays out.
The king asks his advisers in amazement to have the fact confirmed, and they answer: "Certainly, O king." It is a real question that gets an answer, not plainly a question that only makes a point.

The BSB has a statement here: "There is no one who can restrain His hand or say to Him, 'What have You done?'" The marked words start at a relative clause, not a question. The quoted "What have You done?" is a challenge no one can make, not a question the speaker asks.

The officials ask the king to confirm his decree, and he gives a real answer: "According to the law of the Medes and Persians the order stands." It is a leading question in a story, not plainly a figure.

After "Israel is as obstinate as a stubborn heifer", the question "Can the LORD now shepherd them like lambs in an open meadow?" plainly expects the answer no and is not asking for information. It is the BSB's lines 3 and 4. The marked words began with the stray period that ends line 2, so they are trimmed.
In the BSB, "Did not the battle in Gibeah overtake the sons of iniquity?" is a question that expects the answer yes. The span is trimmed to drop the stray ". " at its start. There are no tags.
Both questions in the verse plainly expect yes and make a point. The span is now each whole question, instead of the piece that began with a stray comma. There are no tags.
"who will not fear?" and "who will not prophesy?" both mean everyone will. The stray dash is dropped from the span, and the second question, which has the same shape, is added. There are no tags.

Both questions plainly expect no, and the verse sets them against "But you have turned justice into poison". The span is trimmed to drop the stray "? ", and the first question is marked too. There are no tags.

"Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?" is a boast in the form of a question: it says they did. The extra spans "you who rejoice" and "and say" do not carry the figure. Of the tags, only H3808 is right; H8056, H3810 (twice) and H0559 are not, so the tags are dropped.

Both questions plainly expect yes. The repeated piece "Are you not like" and the broken fragment "I not bring Israel" are replaced by the two whole questions. Both H3808 tags (words 0 and 9, each ha-lo) point at the questions.
"will I not destroy the wise men of Edom...?" is a threat that means "I will". The stray ", " at the start is dropped, and so is the repeated piece "will I not". The H3808 tag on ha-lo is right.

In "is this not what I said while I was still in my own country?" Jonah is stating that he said it. The spans "So he prayed to the LORD", "saying" and "O LORD" do not carry the figure. Every tag except H3808 sits on those words, so the tags are dropped.

The verse answers its own questions with questions that expect yes ("Is it not Samaria?", "Is it not Jerusalem?"). The statement line "All this is for the transgression of Jacob..." is not the figure, and the main span began with a stray "? ". Most tags sit on that statement while the two ha-lo words are untagged, so the tags are dropped.

"Should it be said...?" expects no and "Do not My words bring good to him who walks uprightly?" expects yes; both are plainly questions that tell. "O house of Jacob" is only the address. Tags H1004M, H3290, H7307J, H3068G and H0428 do not carry the question, and the ha-lo of the clearest question is untagged, so the tags are dropped.

"Should you not know justice?" expects yes and rebukes the leaders. The spans "Then I said", "Hear now" and "O leaders of Jacob" are not the figure, and the main span began with a stray ". ". Every tag sits on those words while the question's ha-lo is untagged, so the tags are dropped.

"Is not the LORD among us?" is the leaders' confident question expecting yes. The three marked statement lines about bribes, price and money are not the figure. All the tags fall on those lines and the ha-lo is untagged, so the tags are dropped.

"who will grieve for her?" and "Where can I find comforters for you?" both plainly mean there is no one. The stray "; " is dropped from the span, and the second question, which works the same way, is added. There are no tags.
"So why do You tolerate the faithless?" is Habakkuk's complaint to God. He then waits for God's reply (2:1), and God answers (2:2). It may be a real question asked in distress, so it is not plain.

"Will not all of these take up a taunt against him" expects yes, and "How long will this go on?" is the taunt's mocking cry, not a request to know. "What is not his" is not a question. H3808 also tags the lo' of "not his", not only ha.lo', so the tags go.

"Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?" plainly expects yes. The other marks are pieces of the first question, and one begins with a stray "?". The tags fall on "who", "house", "this", "glory" and object markers and miss ha.lo'.

The question plainly expects yes, and the fathers' own confession follows. "Just as" belongs to their reply, not to the question. The tags cover 'akh, the nouns, the object marker and "prophets" but miss ha.lo'.

"How long, O LORD of Hosts, will You withhold mercy...?" is the angel's plea, and the LORD answers it with kind and comforting words (1:13). It reads as a real plea, not plainly a question that only makes a point.

"Is not this man a firebrand snatched from the fire?" plainly expects yes. The mark begins with a stray "!". "And the LORD said to Satan", "The LORD rebukes" and "Satan" are not the question. The tags fall on said, YHWH, to, the accuser and rebuke, not on ha.lo'.

"Do you not know what they are?" gets a real answer, "No, my lord," and the angel then explains, so it is a real question in a dialogue. The marks and the tags (answered, angel, said, to me, the answer "no") are not the question.
"What are you, O great mountain?" plainly scorns the mountain and is not asking. The mark ran on into the statement "Before Zerubbabel you will become a plain," which is not the question.

"Do you not know what these are?" is answered "No, my lord," and the angel explains in 4:14, so it is a real question. The marks "he inquired" and "No" and the tags on said, to me, saying and no are not the question.

Inside the rebuke begun in 7:5, "were you not doing so simply for yourselves?" plainly expects yes. The main mark began with a stray comma and overlapped the setting clause. The tags take in the two "and if" words of that clause as well as ha.lo'.

"Was not Esau Jacob's brother?" plainly expects yes and leads into "Yet Jacob I have loved." "I have loved you", "says the LORD" and "But you ask" are not that question. The tags cover loved, object markers, says, YHWH, you say and how, beside ha.lo'.

"is it not wrong?" (said twice) plainly expects yes, and after "Try offering them to your governor!", "Would he be pleased with you or show you favor?" plainly expects no. The mark began with a stray comma.
"How can we return?" is the people's reply to "Return to Me," and God answers it in 3:8 ("In tithes and offerings"). The verse does not make plain whether it is a retort or a real question.
"Will a man rob God?" plainly expects no. The second mark, "Yet you are robbing Me!", is God's statement after the question, not the question.

"what are you doing more than others?" expects "nothing" and "Do not even Gentiles do the same?" expects yes. Both plainly make the point. The old mark began with the stray "?" of the question before.
"Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothes?" plainly expects yes and gives the reason for "do not worry". The mark began with a stray period.
"Are you not much more valuable than they?" plainly expects yes, after "your heavenly Father feeds them." The mark began with a stray period.
"will He not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?" plainly expects yes, reasoning from the grass of the field. The mark began with a stray comma.
After "You of little faith," "why are you so afraid?" is plainly a rebuke, not a request for reasons. The mark also took in the address and the narration "Jesus replied".

Read in the BSB with "Have You come here to torture us before the appointed time?", "What do You want with us, Son of God?" sounds like a fearful real question. Without being told the idiom, a reader would not plainly see a question that is not asking.
Jesus "knew what they were thinking," so "Why do you harbor evil in your hearts?" plainly rebukes and does not ask to learn. The mark also took in the narration before the question.
